# Statistics in a nutshell {#sec-nutshell}

## What is statistics? {#sec-what-is-statistics .smaller}

In a nutshell, you may think of statistics as counting.

- **Counting values.**
  How many people are 20 years old? How many flips were heads? How many birds were observed?
- **Counting how much you counted.**
  How many observations do we have?
- **Official counting.**
  Births, deaths, unemployment, crime.
- **Counting the ways things could have happened.**
  How much could our count have varied by chance? How many heads would a fair coin give us?

. . .

> Statistics can be thought of as counting, and as reasoning about counts and their possible
> variation.

::: notes
The fourth bullet is the one that carries the rest of the term. Say it slowly.
:::

## Why statistics? {#sec-why-statistics .smaller}

Fundamentally, we want to learn about the world using observations.
Put differently, we want to learn from data.

- **Estimand:** the quantity we want to learn about (what we want).
- **Estimator:** the procedure by which we learn about it (our method).
- **Estimate:** the result that procedure gives us (what we get).

. . .

**Inference** is using *known* information to *infer* something *unknown*.

- Collecting measurements to infer the association between two variables.
- Collecting a random sample to infer something about a larger population.
- Running randomised experiments to infer a potential outcome.

::: notes
Estimand, estimator, estimate. Three words they will hear every week.
:::

## Fundamental issue in statistics {#sec-signal-noise .smaller}

- We want to separate **noise** from **signal**.
- That is, how certain can we be in our estimate?
- Put differently: how certain can we be that an estimated association between two variables is
  a *real world* association, rather than the result of *random* variation during our
  measurement or data collection?
- This is the fundamental challenge and task of quantitative methods in all science.

::: notes
This is the hinge of the whole course. Everything from week 3 onward is machinery for it.
:::

## A question {#sec-question}

> Do students become more confident in statistics as they progress through their studies?

You just filled out the survey, which asked, among other things, for your current semester and
your confidence in reading statistical results.

## Step 1: Clarify the estimand {#sec-estimand .smaller}

What precisely do we want to learn about?

> The association between semester of study and reported confidence on a 1 to 10 scale.

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
**An association is not a causal effect.**
Nobody was assigned a semester, so we are comparing different people rather than following one
person through their degree.
Causal identification is a separate course.
:::

::: notes
Students reach for the causal sentence by reflex. Correct it here, once, hard.
:::

## Step 3: Formal model {#sec-model .smaller}

Given our approximately continuous outcome, and for the sake of simplicity, we use a bivariate
linear model.

<!-- The whole derivation is one dense block, sized at ladder step 2 (STYLE.md section 5.1) so
     that the slide still fits the canvas with both readings opened. -->
:::: {.small}

**Outcome family**

$$
\text{Confidence}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma)
$$ {#eq-likelihood}

<!-- A callout's own collapse="true" is silently ignored by the revealjs format, so the
     collapsible readings in this deck are wrapped in a <details> block instead. That is the
     same disclosure widget as the "View source" folds, and theme.scss already sizes it. -->
<details>
<summary>How to read the outcome family</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**@eq-likelihood in words.**
We assume the outcome, the reported confidence of student $i$, to be normally distributed with mean $\mu_i$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.
:::

</details>

**Linear predictor**

$$
\mu_i = \alpha + \beta \times \text{Semester}_i
$$ {#eq-linear-predictor}

<details>
<summary>How to read the linear predictor</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**@eq-linear-predictor in words.**
We model the mean confidence score as a function of the reported semester.
$\alpha$ is the baseline level of reported confidence for a hypothetical semester 0 student, the intercept.
$\beta$ is the average change in reported confidence per unit change in semester, and it is therefore our estimand, the slope.
Everything the semester does not account for is the residual spread, which is the $\sigma$ of @eq-likelihood.
:::

</details>

::::

## Step 3: The posterior {#sec-posterior .smaller}

$$
P(\alpha, \beta, \sigma \mid \text{Data}) \propto \mathcal{L}(\alpha, \beta, \sigma \mid \text{Data}) \times P(\alpha, \beta, \sigma)
$$ {#eq-posterior}

<details>
<summary>How to read the posterior</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**@eq-posterior in words.**
The probability of our model parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\sigma$) *given* the data we collected, here the confidence and semester answers, is proportional to the likelihood, a function assessing the plausibility of different parameter values given our data, multiplied by the prior distributions of those parameters.
:::

</details>

. . .

The posterior is a full probability distribution, not a single number.

::: notes
This equation is the whole course in one line. They meet it again in week 3 and week 7.
:::

## Step 3: The priors {#sec-priors .smaller}

A prior is a probability distribution over a parameter before seeing the data.
I chose:

:::: {.small}

$$
\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(5, 2), \qquad \beta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2), \qquad \sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(1)
$$ {#eq-priors}

<details>
<summary>How to read the prior on the intercept</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**The prior on $\alpha$ in words.**
Before evaluating the observed data, the expected intercept sits in the middle of the outcome scale (5), and with 95 percent probability it is 5 plus or minus about 4.
As in @eq-likelihood, the pair in $\mathcal{N}(5, 2)$ is a mean and a standard deviation, which is also what `brms` expects.
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary>How to read the prior on the slope</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**The prior on $\beta$ in words.**
My prior expectation is that there is *no association*, hence a mean of 0, but with 95 percent probability it lies between -4 and +4, which would be very large effects on a 10 point scale.
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary>How to read the prior on the residual spread</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**The prior on $\sigma$ in words.**
Before knowing anything from the data I know the spread must be positive, so a normal distribution will not do.
Small spreads are a priori more plausible than large ones.
:::

</details>

::::

## Step 3: The priors, drawn {#sec-priors-drawn .smaller}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
priors_drawn <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    parameter = "alpha: the intercept",
    value = seq(-3, 13, length.out = 200),
    density = dnorm(value, mean = 5, sd = 2)
  ),
  tibble(
    parameter = "beta: the slope",
    value = seq(-8, 8, length.out = 200),
    density = dnorm(value, mean = 0, sd = 2)
  ),
  tibble(
    parameter = "sigma: the spread",
    value = seq(0, 8, length.out = 200),
    density = dexp(value, rate = 1)
  )
)

ggplot(priors_drawn, aes(x = value, y = density)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_3, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free") +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Density", title = "What I believe before seeing any answer")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The three priors as pictures. Each curve says how plausible I find each value of that parameter before seeing a single answer, which is why the slope curve is centred on zero and the spread curve never reaches below it.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-priors-1.png){#fig-priors width=5000}
:::
:::


::: notes
Priors are commitments, not conveniences. Centring beta on zero is the honest starting point,
not a trick to get a null.
:::

## Step 4: Prior predictive check {#sec-prior-predictive .smaller}

What data would our prior beliefs produce?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
n_sim <- 500

# One draw from each prior is one possible world. In each world, simulate the answer that one
# student at one semester would give.
prior_data <- tibble(
  alpha = rnorm(n_sim, mean = 5, sd = 2),
  beta = rnorm(n_sim, mean = 0, sd = 2),
  sigma = rexp(n_sim, rate = 1),
  semester = sample(1:10, size = n_sim, replace = TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(confidence = rnorm(n_sim, mean = alpha + beta * semester, sd = sigma))

ggplot(prior_data, aes(x = semester, y = confidence)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.5, xmax = 10.5, ymin = 1, ymax = 10, fill = col_2, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(colour = col_3, alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Semester", y = "Confidence", title = "Answers our priors consider possible")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Five hundred answers simulated from the priors alone, before any real answer was used. The shaded band is the 1 to 10 scale the survey actually offers, so every point outside it is an answer our priors think possible and no student could ever have given.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-prior-predictive-1.png){#fig-prior-predictive width=5000}
:::
:::


::: notes
This is the step people skip and the step that catches a bad prior.
Point at how far past 10 the simulated answers reach.
:::

## Step 5: Fit the model {#sec-fit .smaller}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_priors <- c(
  prior(normal(5, 2), class = "b", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b", coef = "semester"),
  prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma")
)

fit <- brm(
  conf_stats ~ 0 + Intercept + semester,
  data = model_df,
  family = gaussian(),
  prior = model_priors,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  seed = 2026,
  refresh = 0,
  file = here("website", "slides", "data", "week01-fit"),
  file_refit = "on_change"
)
```
:::


We will learn in week 7 what is going on here in detail.

. . .

In short: we update our prior distributions of the parameters by conditioning on the observed
data.
Computationally we simulate many different possible lines and rank them by their relative
plausibility, and what comes back is a distribution of plausible regression lines.

::: notes
Run this live and talk over the compile. R writes Stan, Stan writes C++, the compiler builds a
sampler specific to this model. That wait is the reason week 7 exists.
:::

## Step 6a: MCMC diagnostics {#sec-diagnostics .smaller}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mcmc_plot(fit, type = "trace") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = chain_cols) +
  theme_pubr()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Trace plots for the three parameters. Four searches started in different places and ended up wandering around the same region, which is what a working computation looks like. A line drifting off on its own would be the warning sign.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-trace-1.png){#fig-trace width=5000}
:::
:::


We are assessing the simulation algorithm here, and we will learn how in week 7.

::: notes
Say it twice: this is a statement about the computer, not about whether the model is any good.
:::

## Step 6b: Posterior predictive check {#sec-ppc .smaller}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
pp_check(fit, ndraws = 50) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Confidence", title = "Observed answers against what the model predicts")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Posterior predictive check. The dark line is the confidence we actually observed, the pale lines are datasets the fitted model generates. Where they disagree is where the model is wrong about the world.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-ppc-1.png){#fig-ppc width=5000}
:::
:::


- How well do the estimated parameters, remember that these are distributions, combined with the
  predictor, replicate our outcome?
- Intuition: a model fits a dataset well if it can recover the outcomes well.

::: notes
Expect over-smoothing: the model predicts a continuous bell where the data is ten whole numbers.
Name that. It is honest and it previews week 11.
:::

## Step 7: Interpretation {#sec-interpretation .smaller}



Each additional semester is associated with a change of **0.59** scale points of
confidence, with a 90 percent credible interval from **0.03** to **1.09**.
The posterior puts **95 percent** of its mass above zero.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
line_cloud <- conditional_effects(fit, spaghetti = TRUE, ndraws = 100)

plot(line_cloud, points = TRUE, plot = FALSE)[[1]] +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Semester", y = "Confidence", title = "Lines that survive contact with the data")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![One hundred regression lines drawn from the posterior, with the observed answers on top. The spread of the lines is the honest summary of how far this data settles the question.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-line-cloud-1.png){#fig-line-cloud width=5000}
:::
:::


::: notes
Read the sentence verbatim. Never "proves", never "there is no effect", never "significant".
:::

## Step 7: The estimand itself {#sec-interpretation-beta .smaller}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mcmc_plot(fit, variable = "b_semester", type = "areas", prob = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_2) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "Scale points of confidence per semester",
    y = NULL,
    title = "The posterior for the slope"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The posterior for the slope, which is the estimand named at step 1. The dashed line marks no association at all, and how much of the shape sits to either side of it is the answer to the research question.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-posterior-beta-1.png){#fig-posterior-beta width=5000}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note}
**An interval is the answer, not a decoration on it.**
A point estimate with no width attached is a claim the data cannot support.
:::

## Step 8: Limitations {#sec-limitations .smaller}

- Models are **always** wrong, but some are useful.
- It is always important to reflect on what we can learn and what we cannot learn.

::: notes
Name the concrete ones out loud rather than putting them on the slide.
There are nine of us, which is a class and not a sample of any population.
Almost everyone here is in the same semester, and no method fixes that.
Nobody was assigned a semester, so this compares people, not one person over time.
Self-reported confidence is not skill, and it may even move the other way as you learn how much
there is to know.
The normal likelihood ignores the scale, which is what steps 4 and 6b both showed.
:::

# Recap: the normal distribution {#sec-recap}

## The normal distribution {#sec-normal .smaller}

@eq-likelihood said that every answer is normally distributed.
That distribution has two knobs, and nothing else.

- $\mu$ is the mean, and moving it slides the whole curve left or right.
- $\sigma$ is the standard deviation, and raising it makes the curve wider and flatter.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
normal_curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble(curve = "mean 5, sd 1", x = seq(-2, 12, by = 0.05), density = dnorm(x, 5, 1)),
  tibble(curve = "mean 5, sd 2", x = seq(-2, 12, by = 0.05), density = dnorm(x, 5, 2)),
  tibble(curve = "mean 8, sd 1", x = seq(-2, 12, by = 0.05), density = dnorm(x, 8, 1))
)

ggplot(normal_curves, aes(x = x, y = density, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_1, col_3, col_2)) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Density", colour = NULL, title = "Two knobs, three curves")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Three normal distributions. Changing the mean slides the curve sideways, changing the standard deviation changes how wide it is, and no other shape is available.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-normal-curves-1.png){#fig-normal-curves width=5000}
:::
:::


## The 68 and 95 rule {#sec-68-95 .smaller}

The area under the curve is probability, and for a normal distribution that area always splits
the same way, whatever $\mu$ and $\sigma$ happen to be.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
normal_area <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 13, by = 0.05), density = dnorm(x, 5, 2))

ggplot(normal_area, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(normal_area, x >= 1, x <= 9), fill = col_1, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_area(data = filter(normal_area, x >= 3, x <= 7), fill = col_1, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = col_1, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9)) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Density", title = "68 percent inside, then 95 percent")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![A normal distribution with mean 5 and standard deviation 2. About 68 percent of the area lies within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95 percent within two, which is where the reading of the prior on the intercept came from.](week01_files/figure-revealjs/fig-normal-areas-1.png){#fig-normal-areas width=5000}
:::
:::


This is exactly why $\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(5, 2)$ was read as 5 plus or minus about 4.

## The standard normal {#sec-standard-normal .smaller}

$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, is the reference curve.
Every other normal distribution is that same shape, shifted and stretched.

$$
z_i = \frac{x_i - \mu}{\sigma}
$$ {#eq-standardise}

Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation turns any normal variable into a
standard normal one.
A value of $z_i = 2$ then means the same thing everywhere: two standard deviations above the
mean, which @fig-normal-areas puts at the edge of the 95 percent region.

::: notes
Do not derive anything. The point is only that a standard deviation is a unit of distance.
:::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
